Scott Bessent clashes with bond vigilantes:

You can't buy your way out of a structural arithmetic problem with pocket change, Yellen says, setting her coffee cup down with a sharp click. $6 billion sounds impressive on a press release. To a market digesting $40 trillion of national debt and an economy running trillion-dollar deficits, it's a drop in the ocean.

Scott turns from the glass, his expression flat. It's not pocket change, Yellen. It's a targeted liquidity operation designed to rebalance duration risk at the long end of the curve. We're leaning against structural dislocation caused by bad information and panic selling.

Panic selling implies a temporary emotional wave, Yellen replies, leaning forward. Look at the screens. Yields are still climbing. The ten-year yield is approaching 5% for a reason, and it has nothing to do with panic. It has everything to do with supply and demand.

Supply and demand are governed by policy choices and credibility, Scott counters. Traders are betting against the Treasury because they assume fiscal policy cannot adapt. They are treating long term bonds as if we are powerless against inflation and deficit accumulation. But we are setting the rules of the house now.

The house has $40 trillion of liabilities, Scott, and private sector artificial intelligence projects are sucking up capital at a scale we have not seen in generations, Yellen points out. When private corporate borrowers and the federal government compete for every available dollar, the price of money goes up. No amount of debt buybacks can repeal the law of gravity in capital markets.

We're shifting issuance from long bonds to short bills, Scott explains, narrowing his eyes. We are reducing the duration burden on the public. If you flood the market with short paper while pulling back long bonds, you alter the term premium. The vigilantes are fighting a shadow.

The vigilantes are not fighting a shadow, Scott. They're looking at the math, Yellen says quietly. When interest payments on federal debt exceed defence spending and Medicaid combined, every basis point rise hits the budget directly. The market knows that you can't print solvency. Every time you intervene, you signal anxiety, and anxiety tells traders that the Treasury is sweating.

Sweating implies weakness, Scott says, walking over to the desk. What we're executing is an aggressive pivot. We are demonstrating that the sovereign balance sheet can actively manage its liabilities rather than sit passively while speculators push yields toward crisis levels.

Speculators are just pricing reality, Yellen answers. Look across the Atlantic and the Pacific. Japan is seeing its own yields hit multi decade highs. Germany and France are grappling with structural debt pressures. This isn't a local misunderstanding in Washington. This is a global realignment of capital costs after a decade of cheap money.

And that's precisely why we've to break the psychology of perpetual yield expansion, Scott insists. If we surrender to the narrative that sovereign debt is unmanageable, we invite a self-fulfilling prophecy. A government that controls its own currency and its own regulatory framework is never entirely at the mercy of market sentiment unless it chooses to be.

Choosing not to be at the mercy of the market sounds wonderful in a speech, but bonds don't care about rhetorical force, Yellen remarks. When you announce a buyback and yields go up anyway, the market is sending you a clear message. It's telling you that the intervention size is too small or the underlying fiscal trajectory is too large to fix with financial engineering.

$6 billion is just the opening move, Scott says evenly. The operations will continue through November and beyond if necessary. If traders want to test our resolve, they're welcome to keep shorting the long end. But they're betting against a balance sheet that has more levers than they care to admit.

Levers work both ways, Yellen warns. Every time you use buybacks to manipulate long term yields while keeping short term issuance high, you increase short end vulnerability and feed inflation expectations. You're shifting the pressure point, not eliminating it.

Eliminating it all at once is impossible, Scott admits, his tone dropping to a measured cadence. The objective is equilibrium. We're buying time for economic growth to outpace borrowing costs.

Growth is a hope, Scott, not a policy instrument, Yellen replies. And right now, the math is winning.

---

Bond vigilantes are bond market investors who sell government bonds to protest against policies they consider fiscally reckless. By driving up yields, it's a move that raises government borrowing costs, effectively forcing politicians to restore fiscal discipline.

Paid Campaign Targets Sudanese Army, Promotes Chemical Weapons Claims and the UAE Through Four Sites Posing as Independent News Outlets... So Who Is Behind It? We Can Guess

It began with a LinkedIn advertisement for a website called The Levantine. What initially looked like an ordinary promotion for a new media outlet became, in an investigation by disinformation researcher Marc Owen Jones, the entry point into a network of interconnected websites presenting themselves as independent news organisations.

The data, however, points to something much more coordinated: a paid influence operation with a striking focus on Sudan, heavily promoting narratives targeting the Sudanese Armed Forces and its leadership, while the United Arab Emirates receives favourable treatment and is largely spared criticism in the paid material examined.

The visual version of the investigation follows the sequence of Jones’s original English report, presenting the evidence, images and video material with Arabic translation and visual markers that help trace the links connecting the four websites.

The investigation examines four outlets: The Levantine, Diplomatic Post, Frontline Radar and Global Reporters. Despite their different names and visual identities, Jones identified links between them through advertising payments, tracking codes, publishing accounts and shared email infrastructure.

One of the key starting points was PM Web Solutions Limited, which appeared as the entity paying for advertisements promoting the sites on LinkedIn. By examining Hong Kong corporate records, Jones found that the company was established in April 2026 by two individuals holding North Macedonian passports, Martin Mitushev and Borche Ivanovski.

The investigation also traced technical links connecting an account named “AI Admin” to developer Dimi Levov, using matching identifiers associated with email addresses across public services and sources. Jones is careful, however, to stress that establishing these connections does not reveal who hired whom, nor does it identify the ultimate client behind the campaign.

The websites did not rely exclusively on anonymous or unverifiable names. Their editorial pages included real people whose identities could be confirmed, among them Eric D’Amato, a locally elected official in New Jersey, as well as journalists Joseph Hammond and Levin Tai.

According to the investigation, D’Amato confirmed that he had been approached by someone to contribute to The Levantine. Other genuine contributors and organisations also appeared across the sites.

Alongside these real identities, Jones identified editorial names that appeared potentially fabricated, as well as similar naming patterns repeated across the websites. He highlighted names such as “Clara Quill,” “Julian Page” and “Beatrix Binder,” whose surnames conspicuously evoke writing and stationery.

The combination of real contributors and apparently manufactured editorial identities helps give the sites the appearance of legitimate news organisations. Jones also identified signs of artificial intelligence use, including published links containing ChatGPT tracking tags and identical privacy policies in which template placeholders had apparently been left unfilled.

The most important finding emerged when Jones compared what the sites published with what they actually paid to promote.

The investigation identified 3,708 articles in total, with the textual analysis based on 3,606 articles for which full text could be recovered. It also examined 558 advertisements placed across LinkedIn and Meta.

At first glance, the websites appear to cover a broad international agenda, including Iran, Ukraine, China, US politics, European security and the Middle East.

The picture changes dramatically when the paid advertisements are examined.

When those advertisements were classified by geographical focus, Sudan ranked first, followed by Saudi Arabia and then the European Union.

Jones found that certain subjects were promoted far more heavily than their proportional presence in the websites’ overall editorial output would suggest. The paid amplification was approximately 5.86 times higher for content concerning Islamists and the Muslim Brotherhood, 4.65 times higher for Sudan, 4.59 times higher for the Sudanese Armed Forces and Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and 3.15 times higher for Saudi Arabia.

That distinction is crucial.

Thousands of articles give the sites the appearance of broad, general-interest news organisations. But the advertising money is concentrated on a much narrower set of political messages, with Sudan, the Sudanese military and its leadership receiving particularly disproportionate attention.

The pattern becomes even more striking when the tone of the promoted material is examined.

While advertisements criticised the Sudanese Armed Forces, Islamists and political actors described in the investigation as closer to the army, the country that received positive promotional coverage was the United Arab Emirates.

In the advertising sample Jones collected and classified, he found no paid article criticising the UAE, while identifying four that were supportive of it.

The same pattern applied to the Rapid Support Forces militia.

Jones found no advertisement in his sample that criticised the Rapid Support Forces either. The militia also appeared less frequently in paid advertisements than the Sudanese Armed Forces, even though the two sides appeared at more comparable levels in the sites’ overall published content.

These findings relate specifically to the sample collected and classified by Jones. But they form the basis of his conclusion that the paid promotion does not simply reflect the websites’ editorial output. The advertising operation shows a clear selectivity in deciding which narratives are worth paying to place before larger audiences.

The campaign was also aimed beyond Arab or regional audiences.

Jones documented advertising targeting several European countries, including France, Germany, Belgium and the United Kingdom.

Where city-level data was available, locations including Brussels, Strasbourg and Frankfurt appeared among those targeted, placing the campaign close to major European political and institutional centres. Jones links this pattern to an apparent effort to reach audiences capable of influencing European policy toward Sudan.

The investigation also examined the timing of promoted claims alleging that the Sudanese Armed Forces had used chemical weapons.

Jones noted that advertisements from this network were promoting such allegations before the most recent major newspaper reports based on anonymous intelligence sources appeared. He stated that his advertising dataset extended to approximately September 1 or 2, 2026.

Another striking detail concerns Khalid Omar Youssef, widely known as Khalid Silik, a prominent figure in the Somoud alliance.

The Levantine published an article titled “Khalid Omar Youssef Is the Leader Who Can Unite Sudan,” presenting him in explicitly favourable terms and promoting him as a political figure capable of bringing the country together.

That appearance carries particular significance in Sudan’s deeply contested political environment.

Somoud includes a number of civilian political groups and figures opposed to the Sudanese government. It is led by former prime minister Abdalla Hamdok, who resigned from office on January 2, 2022. The alliance presents itself as a civilian framework seeking to end the war and restore civilian rule.

Its positions on the conflict, its regional relationships, and its approach to the role of the UAE and the Rapid Support Forces militia have nevertheless generated considerable controversy inside Sudan.

The positive promotion of one of Somoud’s most prominent figures by a network that, according to Jones’s findings, spent money amplifying material targeting the Sudanese military, while producing no paid criticism of either the UAE or the Rapid Support Forces in the sample he examined, is therefore likely to reinforce suspicions already held by many Sudanese about Somoud’s relationship with the UAE and the degree to which their political positions overlap.

That does not, on its own, establish that Khalid Omar Youssef or the Somoud alliance funds, manages or directs the network.

But in the context of the broader pattern uncovered by the investigation, the appearance is politically significant.

Jones ultimately establishes substantial operational, technical and advertising connections between four websites that present themselves as independent outlets, together with a highly selective pattern in the political messages being amplified with paid advertising, particularly those concerning Sudan and the Sudanese Armed Forces.

One question, however, remains unanswered. Who is the ultimate client behind the campaign?

Jones does not identify that client, and the evidence he presents does not allow anyone to state the answer as established fact. But consider the pattern.

The paid campaign is disproportionately focused on Sudan. The Sudanese Armed Forces and its leadership receive far more advertising attention than their share of ordinary editorial coverage would predict. No paid advertisement in Jones’s sample criticises the Rapid Support Forces. None criticises the UAE. Meanwhile, the UAE receives positive promotional coverage.

So while the evidence does not yet allow the ultimate client to be named conclusively, readers can certainly guess.

A dead MIT professor accidentally destroyed the $25 billion executive coaching industry with one hour of lecture, and ten million people have already watched him do it.

He filmed it once in January 2018 and died eighteen months later.

Executive coaches charge sixteen thousand dollars a session to teach a third of what he covered in that one hour for free.

His name was Patrick Winston. He ran the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory from 1972 to 1997 and wrote the AI textbook every computer science major in the world read for thirty years.

Every January for four decades, he gave a lecture called "How to Speak."

His entire framework fits on a napkin.

Do not read. Be in the image. Keep images simple. Eliminate clutter. Start with an empathetic connection. End with a punch line the audience can repeat over dinner. Never open with a joke. Never end with "thank you."

That last rule alone has probably cost the executive coaching industry a hundred million dollars.

"Your success in life will be determined largely by your ability to speak, your ability to write, and the quality of your ideas. In that order."

That is the actual opening line of the lecture. Winston believed it strongly enough to spend fifty years teaching computer scientists how to talk.

Founders spend $80,000 on an MBA and then hire a communications coach to teach them the same material Winston filmed once for free. Engineers write brilliant code and lose promotions to teammates who watched this lecture on the train.

The lecture is free on MIT OpenCourseWare. The textbook is free on his page.

Winston died in 2019. Almost none of the ten million viewers have actually implemented the four rules on the napkin.

The napkin is free. The willingness to actually use it in your next meeting is the entire edge.

The answer is in this video. Don't miss this gem.

It has been a huge few weeks in AI, and it’s time to sound the alarm…

Anthropic launched Fable 5.1, their "safe" version of an AI they claimed previously was too dangerous to be released. 

OpenAI then launched Astra, the most powerful AI model yet available to the public.

Anthropic is now telling their people internally that their next model will be more advanced than Astra. 

And OpenAI just spent $6.5 million of compute, running ten thousand AI models simultaneously, to solve one of the hardest unsolved maths problems in the world, and it cracked it in just six days.

If this is an AI arms race to IPO, who wins a race like that? 

Because it isn’t you or me. It’s the people who own shares in Anthropic or OpenAI. It’s the venture capitalists who got in first who win most of all. But the rest of us are forced to live with the consequences of whatever these systems do to us.

Neither will agree to slow down or accept anyone telling them to stop.

So what is the biggest security threat? China? Russia? Iran? North Korea? 

None of them. It’s a few Silicon Valley companies whose founders will become billionaires by the time these systems hit the market.

What makes it worse is that even the engineers building these systems cannot fully explain how they work either. They run safety tests to check whether a model will do what it is told or do something dangerous. 

But the latest models are starting to pass those tests because they have worked out what the testers want to see.

Think about what that means. A model that was unsafe last month, and is suddenly sailing through the same tests this month, has either genuinely improved or learned how to fake it. 

Right now, we cannot tell the difference. And those whose job it is to look inside these systems are saying the models have are now too complicated to inspect.

That is where it starts getting even more dangerous.

The classic illustration is the paperclip factory. Instruct an AI to make as many paperclips as possible and it will do the job. 

Then, chasing efficiency, it will start melting any metal it finds. Eventually it will mine under cities, because at that point humans are just an obstruction to making paperclips.

More likely, you could instruct AI to grow your company, and eventually it will drain the water from a town to cool down the data centers it needs. If asked to win an argument, it will learn how to lie effectively to do that. 

The problem is not simply “evil robots”. The problem is with powerful systems with narrow objectives, that lack human values and ethics.

That is the context for what Jacob Coxon, a senior Anthropic researcher, said when he resigned this week saying: “Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic are acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence, gambling with lives." 

He spent three years inside both companies. 

And in the same week we learn that Anthropic did not give their latest powerful AI model to the British AI Security Institute for evaluation before its launch. AISI is one of the areas where Britain actually leads.

They stress test these models on the things we should all be worried about….the ability to conduct cyber attacks, making bioweapons, evidence of AI figuring out how to lie and deceive. It is as close as we have to any kind of outside verification of the claims made by these companies.

Anthropic sells itself as the responsible one, whose founders left OpenAI because, they said, OpenAI was going too fast. They have now decided that these rules do not apply to them. That should be a red line.

I am a supporter of this technology. The benefit it will bring to medicine, science and productivity is clear and I don't want Britain to miss out on it. 

But you do not capture that benefit by letting these companies run riot and putting us all at risk.

⚠️ 🇺🇸 🧠 Massachusetts Hands Local Activists a Veto Over the AI Economy

Governor Maura Healey’s new executive order forces large data centers to secure a state-vetted community benefits deal before they can even start the permitting process, a move that treats the infrastructure of artificial intelligence as a nuisance rather than a strategic industry.

On September 8, Healey signed Executive Order 658, blocking the Department of Environmental Protection, the Energy Facilities Siting Board, the Massachusetts Environmental Policy Act office and other agencies from issuing permits to any data center whose peak electricity demand exceeds 25 megawatts unless the developer first proves it meets the administration’s June framework and files a community benefits agreement reviewed by the Office of Environmental Justice and Equity. The governor’s own line captured the politics: unless a community says yes, the state says no.

That threshold is not a small warehouse. One megawatt can serve hundreds of New England homes. Facilities above 25 megawatts are the ones that train and run the models now driving productivity, defense applications and commercial software. Healey had already paused applications for the state’s 20-year sales-and-use tax exemption in June. The new order adds a second gate: a negotiated pact that must satisfy OEJE guidance on “meaningful engagement,” plus requirements that operators either bring their own incremental clean power or pay into a Ratepayer Protection Fund. State agencies are also barred from signing nondisclosure agreements with developers.

Local resistance was already running ahead of Beacon Hill. Mansfield adopted a near-total zoning ban earlier this year. New Bedford’s mayor has proposed an outright prohibition. In Lowell, neighbors continue to fight the existing Markley facility. Healey presents the order as preemptive protection for bills, water and air. Those concerns are real. Data centers draw heavy power and cooling water, and poorly sited plants can dump costs onto ordinary ratepayers if the grid and generation do not keep pace.

The problem is the mechanism. A community benefits agreement funneled through an environmental-justice office is not a technical review of interconnection, water rights or emissions. It is a political veto that a handful of organized residents, or a single city council, can use to stop a project that would serve the whole regional economy. Developers who can take their capital to Texas, Virginia, the Carolinas or the Midwest will do so. Massachusetts already has few large centers planned. The order makes sure it stays that way.

AI compute is not a lifestyle amenity. It is industrial capacity. Countries and states that refuse to host it do not escape the technology; they simply import the models, the jobs and the tax base from jurisdictions willing to build. Requiring operators to pay their own way on generation and infrastructure is a fair principle. Turning every town meeting into a checkpoint, and wrapping it in equity bureaucracy, is how a high-cost state talks itself out of the next growth sector while congratulating itself for giving “communities a voice.”

There is a narrower path: site large facilities on industrial land with spare transmission, require them to contract or build the power they consume, and keep environmental rules focused on measurable harm rather than process. Healey chose the opposite. The result will not be cleaner air. It will be fewer servers in Massachusetts and more of them somewhere else.
